faq.q: Which algorithms are available, and are HMAC and MD5 both supported?
faq.a: It computes MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. SHA-1/256/384/512 use the browser's built-in Web Crypto (crypto.subtle); MD5 is not part of Web Crypto so it uses the SparkMD5 library. HMAC (keyed hashing) is offered for SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 — enter a secret key and those rows switch to HMAC. There is no HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA1 row because the tool deliberately keeps HMAC on the strong algorithms.

faq.q: How is text hashed, and what does the 'trim trailing newline' option do?
faq.a: Text is encoded as UTF-8 with TextEncoder before hashing, so non-ASCII characters (accents, Devanagari, emoji) are hashed as their real UTF-8 bytes — matching what hashlib or sha256sum produce for the same string. Editors and shells often add a newline at the end of a file; the 'Trim one trailing newline' checkbox removes a single trailing \n or \r\n so your result can match a command-line checksum that was taken without it.

faq.q: Can it hash a 1 GB file without freezing or uploading it?
faq.a: Yes for MD5 and SHA-256: the file is read in 4 MB slices and hashed incrementally, so it is never fully loaded into memory and a progress bar updates as it goes. Nothing is uploaded — the file is read locally. SHA-1, SHA-384, SHA-512 and file HMAC are computed over the whole file via Web Crypto and are limited to files up to 512 MB, with an on-screen message when a file is larger, because those paths read the entire file into memory.

faq.q: How does comparing against an expected hash work?
faq.a: Paste the hash you expect — hex (any case) or Base64 — into the Compare box. It is normalised and checked against every computed digest on the page, so you do not have to pick the algorithm yourself. A green banner names the algorithm that matched; a red banner means it matched none of them. This is the quick way to verify a downloaded file against a vendor's published checksum.
